label: A Plan Presented as a Strategy
summary: The artefact is a set of dated, resourced actions the organisation intends to take. Nothing in it depends on how anyone outside the organisation responds.
signals: Structured as workstreams, milestones, owners and dates
Success is defined as completing the activities
No competitor appears anywhere in the document
Every element is within the organisation's unilateral control
why_costly: Execution can be flawless while the organisation still loses, because no claim was ever made about why customers would choose it.
coaching_move: Do not tell them it is a plan. Ask which part could fail even with perfect execution, and let the absence of an answer do the work.

label: How-to-Win as a List of Initiatives
summary: The How-to-Win is a portfolio of individually sensible improvements that does not add up to a reason a customer would choose this organisation over another.
signals: How-to-Win reads as a numbered list of programmes
Items are joined by 'and' rather than by 'therefore'
Removing any single item would not break the rest
The implied claim is being somewhat better at many things
why_costly: Investment spreads evenly, no advantage compounds, and the organisation ends up distinctive at nothing.
coaching_move: Ask what the list implies about the customer's decision, then ask which one item the whole logic depends on.

label: Aspiration Standing In for Strategy
summary: A vision, purpose statement or ambition occupies the place where choices should be, with no arena and no way of winning specified.
signals: Language of being the leading, trusted, preferred or best-in-class provider
No named customer, arena, or competitor
Would be signed by every competitor without amendment
why_costly: Gives no guidance on any actual decision, so daily choices continue to be made on precedent and preference.
coaching_move: Ask what winning would look like such that a specific competitor had clearly lost.

label: Targets Substituting for Choices
summary: The strategy is a set of numbers - growth, margin, share - with no account of the market position that would produce them.
signals: Aspiration expressed entirely as financial or share metrics
The path to the number is a growth rate, not a choice
Same document would serve any arena
why_costly: Numbers cannot arbitrate between two arenas or two ways of winning, so the hard choices remain unmade while everyone feels aligned.
coaching_move: Ask what has to become true in the market for that number to appear, and for whom the organisation is winning when it does.

label: An Arena That Excludes Nothing
summary: Where-to-Play describes everything the organisation currently touches, or everywhere it could imagine going, with no exclusions.
signals: Customer definition is a whole market or 'anyone who needs X'
No segment, geography or channel is ruled out
Exclusions named are ones the organisation could not serve anyway
why_costly: Capabilities and systems cannot be configured for advantage in an unbounded arena, so the organisation competes as a generalist against specialists.
coaching_move: Ask which customers the organisation would be content for a competitor to take, and what it would decline if offered tomorrow.

label: Inherited Arena Left Unexamined
summary: Significant parts of Where-to-Play - typically channel, intermediaries, or position in the value chain - were never chosen, only continued.
signals: Channel and route to market are absent from the strategy
Intermediaries are treated as logistics rather than as customers with their own interests
The arena matches the organisation chart
why_costly: The unexamined part of the arena silently constrains the How-to-Win, and the party standing between the organisation and its customer has its own strategy.
coaching_move: Ask which parts of the arena this team chose and which were simply always there.

label: Segments That Do Not Explain Behaviour
summary: Customers are segmented by size, industry, region or demographic category - convenient for reporting, but unrelated to why anyone chooses anything.
signals: Segments are cut by revenue band, headcount, geography or age
No account of what these customers are trying to accomplish
The differentiated offer is the same for every segment
why_costly: A How-to-Win aimed at a segment that shares no behaviour cannot be sharp, because there is no common decision to win.
coaching_move: Ask what these customers do differently from the ones excluded, and what they are trying to get done when they choose.

label: No Customer in the Strategy
summary: The strategy describes what the organisation will build, become or improve, without naming whose behaviour must change for any of it to matter.
signals: Customer referred to only as 'the market', 'users', or 'stakeholders'
No promise stated in customer-facing language
Success measures are all internal
why_costly: If nobody has identified the action being sought, there is no way to tell whether the strategy is working until the revenue does or does not arrive.
coaching_move: Ask what a specific customer would do differently on a specific day if this strategy succeeded.

label: Difference the Customer Will Not Pay For
summary: The claimed differentiation is real but does not change customer behaviour at the point of choice, so it produces cost without advantage.
signals: Differentiators are features the organisation is proud of
Evidence is internal opinion or awards rather than customer choice
No claim about willingness to pay, switching or retention
why_costly: The organisation carries the cost of being different and collects none of the return, which is worse than being undifferentiated and cheap.
coaching_move: Ask what customers give up elsewhere in order to have this, and how the team knows.

label: Claiming Both Cost and Differentiation
summary: The strategy promises to be both the low-cost option and the premium one, which usually means neither set of trade-offs has been accepted.
signals: Best quality at the best price, stated without a mechanism
No activity is being given up to fund either position
Cost programme and premium programme running in parallel
why_costly: Leaves the organisation attackable from both directions by competitors who have made a choice.
coaching_move: Ask which of the two the organisation would protect if it could only keep one, and what that implies for next year's budget.

label: Best Practice as a How-to-Win
summary: The way of winning is to adopt what leading players in the arena already do, which by construction cannot produce advantage over them.
signals: Benchmarking against industry leaders as the central logic
Goal expressed as closing gaps to peer performance
Nothing in the strategy a competitor would find surprising
why_costly: Convergence to the same practices removes the basis for customer preference and shifts competition to price.
coaching_move: Ask what this strategy asks the organisation to do that its strongest competitor would refuse to do.

label: Assuming a Permanent Barrier
summary: Advantage is treated as a structural moat that holds once built, which licenses underinvestment in the learning that would keep it alive.
signals: Advantage described as a durable barrier requiring no renewal
No account of how the advantage could erode
Competitor analysis frozen at the current state
why_costly: Positions that are not re-earned decay quietly, and the organisation notices only when the erosion reaches the financials.
coaching_move: Ask what would have to happen for this advantage to be worth less in three years, and who would have to notice first.

label: A Strategy With No Competitor In It
summary: The logic runs entirely through the organisation's own actions and capabilities, as though rivals will neither respond nor already be there.
signals: Competitors mentioned only in a landscape slide
No named rival response to the strategy
Market share gains assumed without saying from whom
why_costly: Share comes from somebody, and that somebody gets a vote. Ignoring it makes the plan's arithmetic fictional.
coaching_move: Ask whose customers these are today, and what that competitor does the morning after this becomes public.

label: Capabilities Untethered From the Way of Winning
summary: A list of capabilities the organisation would like to have, most of which would appear in any competitor's list and none of which is traced to the How-to-Win.
signals: Capabilities named at the level of 'digital', 'talent', 'data'
No capability would be dropped if the How-to-Win changed
No account of how gaps get closed, or of what gets defunded
why_costly: Investment goes to general improvement rather than to the few activities that would create advantage.
coaching_move: Ask which capability becomes pointless if the How-to-Win changes, and which two only work because of each other.

label: Assuming the Capability Will Appear
summary: The How-to-Win requires something the organisation cannot currently do, and the strategy neither acknowledges the gap nor says how it closes.
signals: Required capability stated as an intention with no plan, budget or owner
Timeline assumes competence from the start
History of similar builds is not mentioned
why_costly: The most common single point of failure inside otherwise coherent strategies, and it surfaces late.
coaching_move: Ask which required capability the organisation has never demonstrated, and what evidence exists that it could build it in time.

label: Choices With No Supporting Systems
summary: The choices are made but nothing in the measures, budgets, reviews or incentives changes to build or protect them.
signals: Management systems box empty or filled with 'governance'
Same metrics, same budget shape, same meeting agendas as last year
No named owner for any choice
why_costly: The organisation reverts to whatever the existing systems already reward, and the strategy becomes a document people remember fondly.
coaching_move: Ask what is different on Monday morning: which measure, which budget line, which standing agenda item.

label: Measuring Only the Outcome
summary: The only indicators are financial results, which report on the strategy long after the point at which it could have been corrected.
signals: All KPIs are revenue, margin, cost or share
No indicator attached to any critical assumption
First review point is a year out
why_costly: The organisation learns its theory was wrong from the income statement, when the cheapest correction window has closed.
coaching_move: Ask which observable thing would move first if the strategy were working, and which if it were quietly failing.

label: Logic Never Reverse-Engineered
summary: Nobody has asked what would have to be true for this to be a great choice, so the conditions the strategy depends on are neither listed nor ranked by doubt.
signals: Assumptions section absent, or a list of risks with mitigations
No statement of which condition the team believes least
Confidence expressed without reference to any test
why_costly: The organisation cannot tell which part of its theory is load-bearing, so it tests the easy things and bets the company on the doubtful one.
coaching_move: Take the strategy as given and ask what would have to be true about customers, competitors, capabilities and economics for it to be a great choice.

label: One Option, Seeking Support
summary: The work began with a preferred answer and proceeded to justify it, so the choice was never made among genuine alternatives.
signals: Alternatives described only to be dismissed
All options share the same Where-to-Play
The rejected options were never specified enough to evaluate
why_costly: The quality of a decision is bounded by the quality of the alternatives considered, and here there was one.
coaching_move: Ask what the second genuinely different possibility was, and what would have had to be true for it to win.

label: Rigour as Decoration
summary: Elaborate quantification applied to questions the data cannot settle, producing confidence rather than insight.
signals: Multi-year projections to a decimal place
Models extrapolating the past into a different future
No possible output of the analysis would have changed the recommendation
why_costly: Manufactures certainty where judgement was required, and makes the resulting choice harder to revisit because it looks proven.
coaching_move: Ask what result from that analysis would have led the team to a different decision.

label: Analysis as Deferral
summary: More study is commissioned in the hope of removing the need for judgement, and the decision recedes indefinitely.
signals: Next step is always another piece of work
No date by which a choice will be made
Nobody can say what evidence would be sufficient
why_costly: Delay is itself a choice, usually in favour of the status quo, and it is made without anyone owning it.
coaching_move: Ask what decision the next study would change, and what the team would choose if it could never be run.

label: Logic Resting on What Others Should Do
summary: The strategy depends on customers, partners, regulators or competitors behaving as they ought to rather than as their own interests dictate.
signals: Language of 'customers should value', 'the market will recognise'
Partner cooperation assumed without their upside stated
Competitor restraint assumed without a reason
why_costly: The bet is on other people's virtue, which is not a competitive asset.
coaching_move: Ask why that party would act that way if they were purely serving their own interest.

label: Defending the Previous Choice
summary: The current course is protected because it is the current course; the conditions that once justified it are no longer examined.
signals: Original rationale cannot be reconstructed by anyone present
Disappointing results consistently attributed to execution
Discussion of alternatives treated as disloyalty
why_costly: The organisation keeps paying for a theory whose premises have expired, and mistakes persistence for commitment.
coaching_move: Ask what had to be true when this course was set, and which of those conditions still hold today.

label: A Strategy Nobody Can State
summary: The strategy exists as a document and as a shared understanding among the few people who wrote it, and nowhere else.
signals: Cannot be stated without the deck
People two levels down describe something different
No function has translated it into its own choices
why_costly: The thousands of small choices made daily continue to be governed by precedent, so the strategy has no effect on behaviour.
coaching_move: Ask who else could state this in their own words, and what a specific function is now choosing differently.

label: Strategy by Consensus
summary: Every constituency's priority survived into the final document, so nothing was traded and the choices do not constrain each other.
signals: Nobody in the room lost anything they cared about
Multiple stated top priorities
Nothing was defunded to fund the strategy
why_costly: Produces the middle position - neither low cost nor differentiated - with the additional cost of everyone believing they agreed.
coaching_move: Ask who gave something up when this was decided, and what it was.

label: Pilots Standing In for a Choice
summary: A set of small adjacent experiments substitutes for deciding which position to pursue, and their encouraging early results confirm a local direction.
signals: Strategy consists of pilots and options to be revisited later
No statement of which peak the pilots are climbing towards
Success criteria are engagement or learning rather than a decision
why_costly: On a landscape with many peaks, incremental feedback reliably leads to a local summit and away from the ones worth having.
coaching_move: Ask what these pilots could prove, what they structurally cannot, and which choice they are meant to unlock.

label: Words That Survive Any Strategy
summary: The strategy is written in terms - customer-centric, innovative, agile, world-class - that no competitor would contest and no decision could be tested against.
signals: Key claims survive replacing the company name with a competitor's
No number, name, or exclusion anywhere in the core statement
Disagreement is impossible because the meaning is unfixed
why_costly: Unfalsifiable language creates the feeling of alignment while leaving every real disagreement unresolved and every choice unmade.
coaching_move: Substitute the strongest competitor's name into the statement and ask whether it is still false.

label: A Framework Standing In for a Strategy
summary: A borrowed tool - objectives and key results, a scorecard, a canvas, a matrix, a maturity model - occupies the place where the choices should be, and its completeness is mistaken for strategic completeness.
signals: The artefact is organised around a tool's template rather than around choices
Objectives and key results, or a scorecard, presented as the strategy itself
The tool has been filled in completely while no arena or way of winning is stated
Discussion centres on the tool's mechanics rather than on what the organisation will give up
why_costly: The tool's structure supplies a feeling of rigour and completeness, which makes the missing choices much harder to notice than a blank page would.
coaching_move: Ask what question the tool answered, then walk the cascade and ask which choices remain unanswered.

label: Execution as the Standing Explanation
summary: Every disappointing result is attributed to delivery, which protects the strategy from examination and leaves the downstream choices that actually produced the result unexamined.
signals: 'The strategy is right, execution is the problem' as a recurring conclusion
Remedies are consistently about discipline, accountability or pace
Nobody can name a choice made downstream that the strategy should have governed
The strategy has never been revised in response to results
why_costly: It makes the strategy unfalsifiable while directing effort at the people least able to change the outcome.
coaching_move: Ask which specific downstream choice went the wrong way, and what the person making it had to go on.
